newsitem.title: POLAND: POLES SLOW TO CHANGE NFI UNITS TO SHARES.
newsitem.headline: POLES SLOW TO CHANGE NFI UNITS TO SHARES.

text.p: Poles' relative slow conversion of NFI units to shares in each of the 15 National Investment Funds should stay slow unless the funds start trading at a significant premium to the units, analysts said.

They said that otherwise many of the NFI or mass privatisation units, which closed on Tuesday at 137.5 zlotys against the funds' NIF index's 139.1 points, might go unconverted until the units in their paper form lose validity at the end of 1998.

"There has to be some kind of impulse to motivate (conversion). Either there'll be a disproportion between the value of the NFIs and units...or that difference will discount the loss of liquidity during conversion," said Mateusz Andrzejewski, an analyst at brokers Bank Pekao SA.

Analysts said the three days or so brokerages and the National Securities Deposit (KDPW) needed to process the conversion made it risky to order the change and freeze the instrument should its price suddenly jump.
Poles have so far exchanged 5,403,163 units in the mass privatisation scheme into shares of the funds. They have been eligible to exchange their unit into 15 shares, one in each fund, from May 12.
The funds entered the bourse's main market on June 12.
By Monday nearly 16 million of the 25.6 million units purchased had been converted into book-entry form, a step necessary for bourse trade.
Under the programme, shares in about 500 mid-sized companies are allocated to the funds run by foreign and domestic management firms. Each NFI has 31,026,185 shares.
Analysts said the recent mediocre performance by the funds' index and the units may have lulled some unit holders to sleep since a first wave of significant conversion in May and June.

They said if the current rally on the Warsaw bourse extended and NFIs and units joined the uptrend, their profile might be heightened enough for smaller investors to seek to buy and sell shares in the individual funds.

"People aren't talking about NFIs so much. There's been no spectacular growth in units, rather the price has fluctuated -- maybe that's the reason," said Sebastian Buczek, an analyst at ING BSK Asset Management.
